prompt: what does survival of the fittest actually mean
reply: Not “strongest wins” — that is the usual misreading. 🌵 Fittest means best fitted to one particular place at one particular time. A cactus is superbly fit for a desert and hopeless in a swamp; a mango tree is the other way round. Change the environment and you change who counts as fittest. 🥭 [CHIPS]What natural selection is|Where variation comes from[/CHIPS]

prompt: what does dna actually do, step by step
reply: It stores recipes for proteins, and proteins do nearly all the work in a cell. 🧬 A gene is one stretch of the strand: the cell copies that stretch, carries the copy to a ribosome, and the ribosome reads it three letters at a time, adding one amino acid per triplet. Chain those amino acids and you have a protein — an enzyme, a hair fibre, an antibody. [CHIPS]What ribosomes are|What breaks a gene[/CHIPS]

prompt: if every cell has the same dna why is a bone cell different from a brain cell
reply: Same book, different pages open. 📖 Almost every cell carries the full genome, but each type switches most genes off and reads only what it needs — a bone cell runs collagen and mineral genes, a neuron runs genes for ion channels and neurotransmitters. Those switch patterns get locked in as cells specialise, which is why skin does not spontaneously turn into brain. [CHIPS]How cells choose|What stem cells are[/CHIPS]

prompt: why does overusing antibiotics create superbugs

The antibiotic clears out the susceptible ones and hands the survivors an empty field to multiply in. Do that often enough, across hospitals and farms, and resistant strains dominate. It is evolution running in days. prompt: what is the actual scientific definition of alive

prompt: how small can a microscope actually see
reply: Light itself sets the limit. 🔬 A wave cannot resolve anything much smaller than about half its own wavelength, so an ordinary light microscope stops near 200 nanometres — fine for cells and bacteria, useless for a virus. Electron beams have far shorter wavelengths, which is how we got our first images of viruses. Clever modern tricks now sneak past that old limit. [CHIPS]What a nanometre is|Why electrons see more[/CHIPS]

prompt: why do mitochondria have their own dna

More than a billion years ago one cell swallowed one of these and did not digest it, and the partnership stuck. You inherit yours from your mother. Because we selected hard for specific traits every generation, change came fast — thousands of years, not millions. A pug still shares ancestry you can read in its DNA.
